acts.name: The Pattern

narrative.speaker: narrator
narrative.text: Dawn breaks over Vedanta Reserve. Dr. Priya Sharma opens her field journal, her owl companion Pip perched on her shoulder.

narrative.speaker: priya
narrative.text: Alright Pip. Three animals today. The lion, the eagle, and the dolphin. Let's see what they have in common.

narrative.speaker: pip
narrative.text: Hoo! I'll keep watch while you take notes, Doctor!

narrative.speaker: narrator
narrative.text: Priya watches each animal carefully, scratching notes in her journal. After an hour, she pauses and looks at what she's written...

narrative.speaker: priya
narrative.text: Hmm. Every single one of them breathes. Every one of them moves around. And every one of them eats. The lion, the eagle, the dolphin — all three.

acts.observationPrompt: Dr. Priya turns to you and taps her journal.
questions: What do ALL three animals have in common?
If you had to group these shared traits under one label — what would you call that group?
acts.expectedInsight: Learner identifies shared/common traits across all animals — generalization thinking, recognizing a base pattern

acts.name: The Eagle's Secret

narrative.speaker: narrator
narrative.text: The next morning. Priya focuses her binoculars on the eagle, who has settled on a high branch.

narrative.speaker: priya
narrative.text: Let me look at the eagle specifically. It breathes — yes. It moves — yes. It eats — yes. Same as all animals.

narrative.speaker: pip
narrative.text: Hoo! But watch... watch what it does next!

narrative.speaker: narrator
narrative.text: The eagle stretches its massive wings and launches from the branch, soaring effortlessly above the canopy.

narrative.speaker: priya
narrative.text: It flies. The lion doesn't. The dolphin doesn't. The eagle has everything a general animal has... and then something that belongs only to it.

acts.observationPrompt: Priya circles the eagle in her journal.
questions: What traits does the eagle share with ALL other animals?
What does the eagle have that makes it different from the general animal pattern?
In your own words — how would you describe the eagle's relationship to the general 'animal' group?
acts.expectedInsight: Learner articulates the extension relationship: eagle = shared animal foundation + something uniquely its own (is-a pattern with specialization)

acts.name: The Word

narrative.speaker: priya
narrative.text: You've described something very important. You noticed that the eagle automatically gets everything the general animal group has — and adds its own ability on top.

narrative.speaker: pip
narrative.text: Hoo! And programmers noticed the exact same pattern in the real world, Doctor!

narrative.speaker: priya
narrative.text: Exactly, Pip. In programming, when one type automatically receives all the traits and behaviours of another type — and can then add its own — we call this...

narrative.speaker: narrator
narrative.text: She writes a single word in large letters across the page.

narrative.speaker: priya
narrative.text: INHERITANCE.

acts.observationPrompt: The word hangs in the air. Priya looks at you.
questions: Now that you know the name — can you think of another real-world example where something inherits everything from a group and adds something extra of its own?
acts.expectedInsight: Learner can transfer the pattern to a new domain — showing they understand the concept, not just memorized the story

acts.name: First Code

narrative.speaker: priya
narrative.text: Now let's see how Python says what you already understand. Look at this — Animal exists as a class. The eagle inherits from it.

narrative.speaker: pip
narrative.text: Hoo! One blank. You know what goes there. You described it yourself!

narrative.speaker: narrator
narrative.text: The code appears. One fill-in-the-blank.

acts.expectedInsight: Learner fills class Eagle(Animal): — mapping their story understanding to Python syntax

blanks.hint: What group does the Eagle get its shared traits from?

codeReveal.explanation: class Eagle(Animal): tells Python that Eagle is a specialization of Animal. Eagle automatically gets breathe(), move(), and eat() — just like you described.

acts.name: The Copycat Problem

narrative.speaker: narrator
narrative.text: A week later. Priya is watching a chameleon hunt near the river's edge.

narrative.speaker: priya
narrative.text: Every animal eats. I wrote that in Act 1. Open mouth, chew, swallow. That's the general pattern.

narrative.speaker: pip
narrative.text: Hoo... but watch the chameleon, Doctor. Watch very carefully.

narrative.speaker: narrator
narrative.text: The chameleon locks its eyes on a fly. Then — in one lightning movement — its tongue shoots out three times the length of its body, snatches the fly, and retracts. The chameleon never moved its feet.

narrative.speaker: priya
narrative.text: It's not adding a new behaviour. Eating was already there — every animal eats. The chameleon is doing 'eat'... just completely differently.

acts.observationPrompt: Priya underlines 'eat' in her notes twice.
questions: Is the chameleon doing something brand new, or is it doing something every animal already does — just in its own way?

If the chameleon inherited 'how to eat' from the Animal group, but does it completely differently — what do you think happens to the original version? Does it disappear? Or does the chameleon simply do its own version instead?
acts.expectedInsight: Learner understands that the chameleon replaces/specializes an inherited behaviour rather than adding something new — the concept of overriding without the word

blanks.hint: The chameleon's eat() replaces the Animal's eat(). In programming, this is called ____ing.

codeReveal.explanation: When a child class defines a method with the same name as a parent's method, it overrides it. The child's version runs instead. The original still exists in the parent — the child simply chooses its own version.

acts.name: Whisper Back to the Elder

narrative.speaker: narrator
narrative.text: Priya continues watching the chameleon. But she notices something she missed before.

narrative.speaker: priya
narrative.text: Wait. It's not replacing eating entirely. Before the tongue-flick — it still opens its mouth. Like every animal does. It does the normal thing first... then adds its twist on top.

narrative.speaker: pip
narrative.text: Hoo! So it's not throwing the original away. It calls on the elder's way first, then adds its own!

narrative.speaker: priya
narrative.text: Exactly, Pip. It reuses the foundation it inherited... then extends it. I need to capture this differently.

acts.observationPrompt: Priya draws two steps in her journal.
questions: The chameleon does the 'normal' animal eating first — then adds its tongue-flick. How is this different from the chameleon just completely replacing eating with something new?
If you were writing instructions for the chameleon's eating behaviour — how would you describe the two-step process it follows?
acts.expectedInsight: Learner describes the pattern: first do the inherited behaviour, then layer your own on top — the concept behind super() without the word

blanks.hint: This Python keyword lets a child class 'call back' to its parent's version of a method.

codeReveal.explanation: super() is Python's way of saying 'call the parent class version of this method.' The chameleon uses super().eat() to run Animal's eat() first, then adds its own behaviour after — reuse before extend.

acts.name: Born Different

narrative.speaker: narrator
narrative.text: Back at the field station. Priya is logging each animal into her catalogue system.

narrative.speaker: priya
narrative.text: Every animal I log gets a name and a habitat the moment I record it. That's the standard birth record — name and habitat. Required for everything.

narrative.speaker: pip
narrative.text: Hoo! But what about when you catalogued the eagle, Doctor?

narrative.speaker: priya
narrative.text: Ah. The eagle needed an extra field right from the start — wingspan. Not added later. It had to be recorded in the very first entry. The eagle's birth record is the standard one... plus wingspan.

acts.observationPrompt: Priya flips back to the eagle's first entry.
questions: The eagle needs name, habitat, AND wingspan from the very moment it's first recorded. How is this the same pattern you've already discovered — where the eagle gets the standard stuff and adds its own?
When the eagle's entry is created, what should happen first — fill in the standard animal fields, or fill in the wingspan? Does the order matter?
acts.expectedInsight: Learner sees that even initialization follows the inheritance pattern — the child's constructor should handle the parent's required fields first, then its own additions

blanks.hint: The same keyword from Act 6 — call the parent's __init__ to handle the shared fields before adding your own.

codeReveal.explanation: super().__init__() calls Animal's constructor to set up the shared fields (name, habitat) before Eagle adds its own (wingspan). The pattern is exactly the same as Act 6 — call the elder's setup first, then extend.

acts.name: The Family Tree Grows

narrative.speaker: narrator
narrative.text: Priya is organizing her catalogue and realizes her 'Animal' category is getting too broad.

narrative.speaker: priya
narrative.text: Birds have feathers, lay eggs, and have beaks. Not all animals have those... but all birds do. The eagle is really a specialized Bird, not just a direct specialization of Animal.

narrative.speaker: pip
narrative.text: Hoo! So the eagle inherits from Bird, and Bird inherits from Animal?

narrative.speaker: priya
narrative.text: Exactly. It's a chain. The eagle gets 'breathe' from Animal, 'feathers' from Bird, and adds 'sharp talons' itself.

questions: How does a multi-level chain (Animal → Bird → Eagle) help Priya organize her notes better than just having Animal → Eagle and Animal → Sparrow?
If a Bird inherits from Animal, does it need to redefine 'breathe'? What about the Eagle?
acts.expectedInsight: Learner understands multi-level inheritance: a child can inherit from a parent that itself is a child, automatically getting traits from all ancestors.

codeReveal.explanation: In multi-level inheritance, a class inherits from another derived class. Eagle gets methods from both Bird and Animal automatically.
